'''''Mastocarpus papillatus''''', sometimes called '''Turkish washcloth''', '''black tar spot''',<ref name=Slater>{{cite web |url=https://www.pugetsound.edu/academics/academic-resources/slater-museum/exhibits/marine-panel/turkish-washcloth-or-black-tar-spot/ |title=Turkish Washcloth or Black Tar Spot |author=<!--Not stated--> |date=2017  |department=Slater Museum of Natural History |website=Slater Museum of Natural History |series=Marine Panel |publisher=University of Puget Sound |location=Tacoma, WA |language=English |access-date=12 September 2017 }}</ref> or '''grapestone'''<ref name=Lewallen>{{cite book |last1=Lewallen |first1=Eleanor |last2=Lewallen |first2=John |date=21 March 1996  |title=Sea Vegetable Gourmet Cookbook and Wildcrafter's Guide |language=English |edition=1st |location=Mendocino, CA |publisher=Mendocino Sea vegetable Company |publication-date=21 March 1996 |pages=41, 84 |isbn=978-0964764378 |oclc=34314822 |lccn=95-78957 }}</ref> is a species of [[red algae]] in the family [[Phyllophoraceae]].  It is sometimes confused with the distantly related ''Turkish towel'' (''[[Chondracanthus exasperatus]]'') which is of a similar texture but larger. The [[Botanical name#Components of plant names|specific epithet]] ''papillatus'' ('with [[Nipple|papillae]]')<ref name=ChuckG>{{cite web |url=https://www.winternet.com/~chuckg/dictionary/dictionary.137.html |title=Dictionary of Botanical Epithets |last=G. |first=Chuck |year=2005 |website=Dictionary of Botanical Epithets |language=English |access-date=11 September 2017 |quote=papillosus papillosa papillosum with papillae papilla papill noun/f a nipple, teat }}</ref> is due to the nipple-like projections on the female [[gametophyte]] which can give the texture of a [[terrycloth]] [[towel|washcloth]] found at a [[Hammam|hamam]] (Turkish bathhouse).<ref name=Slater />

==Distribution==
Despite the [[common name]], it grows nowhere near [[Turkey]].  It is instead native to the northeastern [[Pacific Ocean]] and commonly can be found in [[California]], [[Oregon]], [[Washington (state)|Washington]], [[British Columbia]], and [[Alaska]].<ref name=iNat>{{cite web |url=https://www.inaturalist.org/taxa/117807-Mastocarpus-papillatus#map-tab |title=Turkish Washcloth (Mastocarpus papillatus) |author=<!--Not stated--> |access-date=11 September 2017  |website=iNaturalist.org |publisher=iNaturalist Network |language=English }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.boldsystems.org/index.php/Taxbrowser_Taxonpage?taxid=53938 |title=Mastocarpus papillatus Taxonomy Browser BOLDSYSTEMS |author=<!--Not stated--> |year=2014–2017 |publisher=Barcode of Life Data Systems (BOLD) |language=English |access-date=11 September 2017 }}</ref>  It has been found growing as far north as the [[Commander Islands]]<ref>Selivanova, O.N. & Zhigadlova, G.G. (2013). Marine benthic algae of the Commander Islands (Pacific Coast of Russia) with checklist Revised in 2012. ISRN Oceanography 2013: 1-12. https://dx.doi.org/10.5402/2013/470185</ref> and the [[Russian Far East]],<ref>Perestenko, L.P. (1996 '1994'). Krasnye vodorosli dal'nevostochnykh more Rossii [Red algae of the far-eastern seas of Russia]. pp. 1-330[331], 60 pls. St. Petersburg: Rossiiskaia Akademiia Nauk, Botanichesk Institut im. V.L. Komarova [Komarov Botanical Institute, Russian Academy of Sciences] & OLGA, a private publishing company.</ref> and as far south as [[Chile]].<ref>Santelices, B. (1989). Algas marinas de Chile. Distribución, ecología utilización y diversidad. pp. 399. Santiago: Ediciones Universidad Católica de Chile.</ref><ref>Ramírez, M.E. & Santelices, B. (1991). ==Habitat==
It grows on [[Rock (geology)|rocky]] [[Substrate (biology)|substrates]] in the high- to mid-[[intertidal zone]]s and has been found growing at depths of 250 m.<ref name=Slater />  Like many red algae species, it uses [[phycoerythrin]] to [[photosynthesis|photosynthesize]] which allows it to grow deeper than plants using other pigments.<ref name=Slater />

==Description==
Turkish washcloth is reddish-brown to almost black, with males paler than females and lacking the signature papillae on the blades.<ref name=Slater />  The blades are branched and small at less than 15 cm long, as one would expect to a plant with a diminutive common name.<ref name=Slater />  The first blades in the spring are thin, purple and lack papillae.<ref name=Lewallen />  Later in the year the thalli dry out and become [[grey]] and lifeless.<ref name=Lewallen />

''[[Mastocarpus jardinii]]'' is a similar species, and can be confused with ''M. papillatus''.<ref name=rocky>{{cite web |url=https://www.eeb.ucsc.edu/pacificrockyintertidal/target/target-species-mastocarpus.html |author=<!-- Not Stated --> |department=MARINe |website=Pacific Rocky Intertidal Monitoring |publisher=UC Santa Cruz |location=Santa Cruz, CA |date=August 18, 2017 |language=English |title=Mastocarpus |access-date=16 September 2017 }}</ref>  ''[[Mazzaella affinis]]'' thalli looks similar in shape and color to male ''M. papillatus'', but are smaller and grow in thick mats and not as individuals.<ref name=rocky />  It also can be confused with other species with ''Petrocelis'' phases {{see below}}, such as ''[[Pikea]]'', other ''[[Mastocarpus]]'' spp., ''[[Ralfisa]]'', and ''[[Hildenbrandia]]'', thought the last two are thinner than the Turkish towel crust.<ref name=rocky />

==Life cycle==
''M. papillatus'' has a relatively complex reproductive cycle.  Male [[gametophyte]]s discharge [[flagellum|nonflagellated]] sperm to drift in the current until they attach to the [[Carpogonium#trichogyne|trichogynes]] of female plants.  There the sperm perform [[mitosis]] without [[cell division]], turning into a [[sperm]]atium.  [[Fertilisation]] then proceeds through a [[fertilization pore]] between the trichogyne and the spermatium.  The [[egg]]s then grow into [[tetrasporaphyte|tetrasporophyte]]s which are more or less copies of their parents.<ref name=Slater />

Alternately, the tetrasporophyte goes through the ''Petrocelis''{{anchor|Petrocelis}} phase (so named as it was thought to be a distinct genus, ''[[Petrocelis]]'', of [[Phyllophoraceae]]) and grows into a crust that looks like spilled [[tar]], inspiring the ''black tar spot'' common name.  The tetrasporophyte undergoes [[meiosis]] and produce [[Red algae#Life cycle|tetrasporangia]] which release spores to germinate elsewhere.  Eventually the crust grows into a typical adult plant.<ref name=Slater />  This [[crustose]] phase is shared by all members of the genus ''[[Mastocarpus]]'' as well as those in ''[[Pikea]]''.<ref name=rocky />

==Ecology==
Turkish washcloth is food for many animals, including ''[[Echinolittorina ziczac]]'', ''[[Littorina]]'', [[Amphipoda]], ''[[Lottia]]'', ''[[Pholis crassispina]]'', ''[[Lottia scutum]]'', [[Trochidae]], ''[[Lacuna vincta]]'', ''[[Stenosoma]]'', ''[[Mopalia swanii]]'', and ''[[Gumboot chiton|Cryptochiton stelleri]]''.<ref name=Wood>{{cite journal |last1=Wood |first1=SA |last2=Russell |first2=R |last3=Hanson |first3=D |last4=Williams |first4=RJ |last5=Dunne |first5=JA |date=August 18, 2015  |title=Effects of spatial scale of sampling on food web structure |journal=Ecology and Evolution |language=English |publication-date=August 18, 2015 |volume=5 |issue=17 |pages=3769–3782 |doi= 10.1002/ece3.1640|pmid=26380704 |pmc=4567879 |doi-access=free }}</ref>

Like the ''[[Porphyra]]'' species used to make [[nori]], ''M. papillatus'' is susceptible to infection by the [[Parasitism|parasitic]] [[oomycete]] ''[[Pythium porphyrae]]'', or red rot disease, which can kill large colonies.<ref name=Slater />  It is also susceptible to infection by ''[[Pythium marinum]]''.<ref name="Kerwin">{{cite journal|last1=Kerwin|first1=James L.|last2=Johnson|first2=Lisa M.|last3=Whisler|first3=Howard C.|last4=Tuininga|first4=Amy R.|title=Infection and morphogenesis of ''Pythium marinum'' in species of ''Porphyra'' and other red algae|journal=Canadian Journal of Botany|date=1 May 1992|volume=70|issue=5|pages=1017–1024|doi=10.1139/b92-126|language=English|issn=0008-4026|oclc=5140406448}}</ref>

==Uses==
Grapestone is [[Edible seaweed|edible]]<ref name=Slater /> and can be cooked in [[soup]]s or [[Stir frying|stir-fries]] but care must be taken as overcooking can turn the plant mushy and [[gelatinous]].<ref name=Lewallen />  This property can be exploited to use it as a [[thickening agent]] like its close relative ''[[Mastocarpus stellatus]]''.<ref name=Lewallen />  Grapestone has a similar flavor to [[Ostreidae|oysters]].<ref>{{cite news |last1=Hillinger |first1=Charles |date=December 25, 1989  |title=Harvest of the Ocean Garden : Agriculture: Picturesque Northern California coastal waters provide some atypical farmers with an almost limitless bounty: seaweed. |url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1989-12-25-fi-878-story.html |department=Business |work=Los Angeles Times |language=English |location=Los Angeles, CA |publication-date=December 25, 1989 |access-date=16 September 2017 |quote=grapestone, a seaweed with an oyster-like taste and covered with crunchy bumps }}</ref>

Grapestone is easily foraged from the shore, but like any wild species [[Overexploitation|overharvesting]] is possible.  By grabbing the longer blades and pulling sideways, the shorter blades and [[holdfast (biology)|holdfast]] may remain on the rock and live on.<ref name=Lewallen />

''M. papillatus'' is also thought to have [[antimicrobial]] properties.<ref name=Slater />
